title: Agent Newsroom: Efficient Chronological Report Generation via Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration
research_question: Can chronological report generation be organized as dynamically scheduled, budget-aware multi-agent collaboration that improves semantic coverage, temporal grounding, and narrative balance while reducing inference cost?
methodology: The paper introduces MAS-TLS, a multi-agent timeline-summarization system organized around a master editor and specialized reporter agents in a star topology. Its collaborative cycle includes editorial assignment, time-anchored evidence-grounded investigation and drafting, cross-agent scrutiny and adjudication, and adaptive orchestration; allocation and scheduling mechanisms are designed to promote coverage and diversity while respecting token and time budgets. The system is evaluated on the Crisis, Entities, and T17 timeline-summarization benchmarks against traditional and LLM-based baselines, using AR-1, AR-2, Date-F1, token use, inference time, temporal-balance, and topical-balance measures. The authors also conduct component ablations and transfer studies across model backbones and languages.

key_findings.finding: MAS-TLS improves most reported semantic-coverage and temporal-grounding measurements across the three benchmarks, although it does not dominate every individual metric; on T17 its AR-2 result is 2.8% below the strongest compared baseline.

On the Entities benchmark MAS-TLS uses 13.8 million tokens and 37,078 seconds, compared with 20.2 million tokens and 39,009 seconds for the strongest efficiency-oriented baseline CHRONOS, while also obtaining higher AR-1.

The reported temporal and topical distribution measures indicate that MAS-TLS produces more balanced timelines, including lower inter-event temporal variation and topic distributions closer to the reference timelines.

Ablation experiments show that removing distinctiveness or the LLM-based ranking/adjudication component causes substantial quality losses, while disabling adaptive scheduling increases token consumption by about 34%.
Across tested model backbones the paper reports less than 8% relative variation in AR-1, and its cross-lingual experiments retain a semantic-coverage advantage over the strongest compared baseline.
Evidence grounding remains imperfect: the authors report unsupported-event rates of roughly 5.3% to 7.9% across the evaluated benchmarks.

limitations: The experiments are retrospective news-style timeline summarization rather than real-time workplace communication streams.
The authors state that substantially different domains and broader multilingual settings may require new retrieval and budget configurations.
Agent roles, prompts, and major interaction patterns are predefined rather than learned or freely adaptive.
The method depends on the quality of available evidence and temporal cues and does not eliminate unsupported inferences.
The paper identifies human-centered faithfulness and usability evaluation as additional work still needed.
The system does not explicitly model workplace lifecycle labels such as new, open, resolved, and superseded work items.
raw_claims: MAS-TLS decomposes chronological report generation among a master editor and specialized reporter agents.
The master editor allocates reporting work while attempting to preserve coverage and diversity.
Reporter agents investigate temporally anchored evidence before producing candidate timeline content.
Candidate material is subjected to cross-agent scrutiny and consolidation to reduce duplication and weak evidence.
Adaptive orchestration changes agent staffing and work allocation under resource constraints.
The system is evaluated on three established timeline-summarization benchmarks.
MAS-TLS improves most semantic-coverage and temporal-grounding results but is not best on every individual metric.
Adaptive scheduling materially reduces token use relative to an ablated system.
The method produces more balanced temporal and topical coverage than the compared systems on the reported balance measures.
A small but nonzero proportion of generated events remains unsupported by the available evidence.
